Securing the High Frontier: The Case for American Territorial Primacy at the Lunar South Pole

Introduction

For five centuries, the nations that controlled the critical geographic chokepoints of their era—the Strait of Malacca, the Cape of Good Hope, the Suez and Panama Canals—shaped the destiny of global civilization. In the twenty-first century, a new chokepoint is emerging, one that will define the next several hundred years of human economic and strategic life: the Lunar South Pole. The Strategic Stakes Are Civilizational, Not Merely Commercial

The Lunar South Pole is not a symbol; it is infrastructure. Water ice at Shackleton, de Gerlache, and surrounding craters is the economic substrate of all future cislunar activity. Whoever refuels there controls the logistics of deep space. Whoever builds the first solar-power infrastructure on the polar ridges sets the technical standards, the communications protocols, and the operational tempo that others must accept.

This is precisely analogous to Britain's nineteenth-century coaling stations. Those who doubt the parallel should recall that the Royal Navy's dominance rested less on the quality of its ships than on a global network of refueling points that no rival could match or displace. The lunar polar ice deposits are finite, concentrated in a small number of specific craters, and irreplaceable. A rival power—particularly the People's Republic of China, which has announced a joint lunar base with Russia and a crewed landing before 2030—that establishes first-mover exclusivity there will enjoy a compounding advantage that becomes effectively permanent.

The Legal Terrain Favors Clarity, Not Ambiguity

Critics will invoke the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, particularly Article II's prohibition on "national appropriation." But the treaty is more permissive than its invocations suggest. It prohibits sovereignty claims over celestial bodies as a whole; it does not prohibit exclusive-use safety zones, long-duration operational areas, or property rights in extracted resources. The 2015 U.S. Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act and the 2020 Artemis Accords have already established, with international buy-in from over forty nations, that resource extraction and "safety zones" around operations are lawful.

The United States should build on this foundation with a doctrine of Exclusive Operational Zones (EOZs) at the lunar poles: publicly declared, generously sized buffer regions around American and allied installations, within which no uninvited activity will be tolerated. This is not appropriation of the Moon; it is the prudent management of specific sites where conflicting operations would be dangerous and where American investment creates legitimate equities. Credible Military Power Is the Only Guarantor

Rules without enforcement are aspirations. The Outer Space Treaty itself has no enforcement mechanism; the Artemis Accords are voluntary. Third, national leadership must articulate, clearly and repeatedly, that unauthorized encroachment on declared EOZs will be treated as a hostile act warranting proportional response. Ambiguity invites testing; clarity prevents crises.

History is unambiguous on this point. The Monroe Doctrine, initially derided as beyond American capacity to enforce, became the foundation of hemispheric peace precisely because the United States eventually built the Navy to back it. Freedom of navigation in the South China Sea today exists only because U.S. carrier strike groups make it exist. A Lunar Doctrine, backed by credible Space Force capability, is the same principle applied to the next domain.

The Moral Case: Who Would You Prefer Set the Rules?

The most powerful argument for American primacy is comparative. The alternative to U.S. leadership is not a pristine international commons governed by reasonable consensus. The alternative is a contest in which the Chinese Communist Party—a regime that has militarized artificial islands in violation of international tribunals, suppresses internal dissent ruthlessly, and explicitly views space as a warfighting domain—sets the operational norms of the cislunar economy.

The choice is not between American dominance and a peaceful commons; it is between an order shaped by democratic norms and one shaped by authoritarian ones.

Is it worth the cost? The cislunar economy is projected to exceed one trillion dollars annually within decades. The cost of building the architecture to secure American primacy is a fraction of what will be lost if another power controls the chokepoints of that economy.

The Lunar South Pole is the first and most important of the high-frontier chokepoints, and the window to establish primacy there is measured in years, not decades. By declaring Exclusive Operational Zones, building the Space Force capabilities to defend them, and signaling with unmistakable clarity that American equities at the lunar poles will be protected—by force if required—the United States can secure for itself and its allies an open, rules-based cislunar order. Historical Precedent: The Doctrine of Discovery and Territorial Expansion

The concept of territorial claims and their enforcement through military means is not new; it is deeply embedded in human history. During the Age of Exploration, European powers claimed vast territories under the Doctrine of Discovery, asserting ownership over newly found lands by planting flags and establishing outposts, often backed by military might. The United States itself benefited from this paradigm, expanding westward through Manifest Destiny, securing resources, and establishing dominance over strategic regions with military intervention when necessary. Sovereignty Among the Stars: The Case for American Territorial Dominance in Space

A Persuasive Essay

Introduction

In the coming decades, the question of who controls the strategic high ground of space will define the trajectory of civilization as decisively as the question of who controlled the seas defined the last five centuries. The Lunar South Pole—with its permanently shadowed craters harboring billions of tons of water ice, its near-continuous solar energy potential, and its position as the gateway to deeper space—represents not merely a scientific curiosity but a resource of incalculable strategic value. Helium-3 deposits on the Moon could power fusion reactors for millennia. Rare earth elements on asteroids could reshape global industry. Whoever commands these resources commands the future.

The United States stands at a crossroads remarkably similar to the one it faced in 1945, when it emerged as the world's preeminent power with a narrow but closing window of strategic advantage. Today, the People's Republic of China has declared its intention to establish a permanent lunar base by the 2030s. Russia has partnered with Beijing on the International Lunar Research Station. Both nations operate under political systems with no meaningful accountability to the liberal international order. To pretend that the cooperative frameworks of the twentieth century—particularly the 1967 Outer Space Treaty—are adequate to govern the coming scramble for celestial resources is not idealism; it is negligence of the highest order.

This essay argues that the United States should assert exclusive territorial claims over the most strategically valuable celestial bodies and locations—beginning with the Lunar South Pole—and should undergird those claims with credible military capability, including the willingness to use force against rival nations or entities that challenge American sovereignty in space. This position is not reckless imperialism. It is the logical extension of strategic realism, historical precedent, the unique moral authority of the United States, and the pragmatic recognition that an unregulated commons in space will produce catastrophic outcomes for humanity.

I. The Outer Space Treaty Is Obsolete

The foundation of the current legal order in space is the 1967 Treaty on Principles Governing the Activities of States in the Exploration and Use of Outer Space, commonly known as the Outer Space Treaty (OST). Article II of the treaty declares: "Outer space, including the Moon and other celestial bodies, is not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, by means of use or occupation, or by any other means."

This language was a product of its time—a Cold War détente mechanism designed to prevent nuclear weapons from being stationed in orbit. It was drafted when human activity on the Moon consisted of unmanned probes, when no commercial space industry existed, and when the exploitation of extraterrestrial resources was pure science fiction. Critically, the treaty was negotiated between two superpowers locked in an ideological struggle, both of whom had strong incentives to prevent the other from claiming celestial territory while neither had the capacity to meaningfully exploit it.

The world of the 2020s and 2030s bears no resemblance to this context. Resource extraction on the Moon and asteroids is no longer theoretical; NASA's LCROSS mission confirmed water ice at the Lunar South Pole in 2009, and multiple national space agencies and private companies are actively developing mining technologies. The two-superpower framework has given way to a multipolar landscape in which China, in particular, does not share the liberal democratic values that underpinned Western treaty-making.

Moreover, the OST has no enforcement mechanism. It relies entirely on voluntary compliance. As history demonstrates without exception—from the interwar naval treaties to the Biological Weapons Convention—agreements without enforcement mechanisms eventually collapse when the strategic incentives for defection become sufficiently strong. China's systematic violation of its commitments in the South China Sea, where it built and militarized artificial islands while insisting it respected international law, offers an exact preview of how it will behave on the Moon. Beijing will establish "research stations," gradually expand them, assert de facto control over the most valuable terrain, and dare the international community to respond. The OST will provide no remedy.

The United States should therefore withdraw from or amend the Outer Space Treaty and replace it with a framework that recognizes the reality of sovereign interests in space. Relying on a fifty-seven-year-old document to govern activities its drafters never imagined is not responsible multilateralism—it is strategic paralysis.

II. Historical Precedent: Control of the Commons Has Always Required Sovereign Power

The argument against territorial claims in space often proceeds from the assumption that space is, and should remain, a "global commons." But history offers a devastating rebuttal to the notion that unregulated commons produce equitable or peaceful outcomes.

The Seas. For centuries, the world's oceans were nominally open to all. In practice, they were dominated by whatever naval power could project force most effectively. The Pax Britannica—the century of relative global stability from 1815 to 1914—was not secured by treaty or international consensus. It was secured by the Royal Navy, which enforced freedom of navigation, suppressed the slave trade, and ensured that no hostile power could dominate critical sea lanes. When British naval supremacy waned, the result was not a peaceful multilateral ocean order but two world wars. The Pax Americana that followed was similarly underwritten by the United States Navy, which to this day operates on the principle that freedom of the seas is guaranteed by overwhelming American force.

Antarctica. The Antarctic Treaty of 1959 is often cited as a model for space governance. Yet Antarctica remains unindustrialized precisely because it lacks resources of sufficient value to tempt great powers into defection. The moment Antarctica harbors resources as valuable as lunar water ice or helium-3, the treaty framework will buckle. Even now, multiple nations maintain overlapping territorial claims on the continent that the treaty merely "freezes" rather than resolves.

The American West. The expansion of the United States across the North American continent followed a pattern in which sovereign claims were established first and legal frameworks developed afterward. The Louisiana Purchase, the Oregon Treaty, the Mexican Cession, and the Alaska Purchase were all acts of sovereign territorial acquisition that preceded the development of the lands they encompassed. The Homestead Act of 1862 further demonstrates that a grants-of-sovereignty model—in which a dominant power allocates territory and protects property rights—was historically far more effective at producing development and stability than an open-commons model.

The lesson of history is unambiguous: valuable commons that lack a sovereign guarantor of order inevitably become contested spaces characterized by anarchy, conflict, and exploitation by the most ruthless actors. Declaring space a commons and hoping for the best is not a strategy; it is an invitation to a new scramble for territory in which the most authoritarian and aggressive states will have the advantage.

III. The Moral Case: American Hegemony Produces Better Outcomes

Critics will object that advocating American territorial claims in space amounts to imperialism. This objection deserves a direct response: not all assertions of power are morally equivalent.

The United States is the world's oldest continuous constitutional democracy. It operates under the rule of law, with an independent judiciary, a free press, robust protections for civil liberties, and democratic accountability to its citizens. Its record is imperfect, as all human institutions are, but the comparison with its principal rival is not close. China operates a one-party authoritarian state that has constructed a surveillance apparatus of unprecedented scope, crushed dissent in Hong Kong, committed what multiple nations and international bodies have characterized as genocide against the Uyghur people, and demonstrated consistent willingness to violate international commitments when they conflict with the Chinese Communist Party's interests.

The question is not whether space will be dominated by one power or another—that outcome is nearly certain given the enormous advantages accruing to whichever nation establishes infrastructure at key locations first. The question is whether that dominant power will be one committed, however imperfectly, to the principles of liberal democracy, free enterprise, and the rule of law—or one committed to authoritarian control, state capitalism, and the subordination of individual rights to party interests.

Under American hegemony in the post-World War II era, the global order—despite its many failures—produced the greatest reduction in poverty, the greatest expansion of political freedom, and the greatest advancement in scientific knowledge in human history. This was not coincidental. American power created the conditions—stable sea lanes, enforceable contracts, deterrence against aggression—under which liberal institutions could flourish.

American dominance of the most valuable real estate in space would produce similar conditions for the space economy. With the United States guaranteeing security of tenure, private companies from allied nations could invest in lunar and asteroid mining with the confidence that their investments would be protected. International scientific collaboration could proceed under an American security umbrella, just as similar collaboration has proceeded on Earth under the NATO alliance. Resource wealth could be developed and distributed through market mechanisms rather than hoarded by authoritarian states for strategic leverage.

The alternative—a space domain in which authoritarian powers control key resources—would produce outcomes as predictable as they are dangerous. A China that controls the Lunar South Pole's water ice controls the ability to sustain human life on the Moon and to produce rocket fuel for deeper space missions. It becomes the gatekeeper of humanity's expansion into the solar system. This is an outcome that no advocate of human freedom should be willing to accept.

IV. The Strategic Imperative: First-Mover Advantage and the Physics of Space Warfare

Beyond the moral and historical arguments, there is a hard strategic reality that must be confronted: in space, geography and physics bestow enormous advantages on the first power to establish a presence at key locations, and these advantages compound over time.

The Lunar South Pole contains specific craters—Shackleton, de Gerlache, Shoemaker, Faustini, and others—that represent the most valuable real estate in the solar system. The permanently shadowed regions within these craters contain water ice that can be converted into drinking water, breathable oxygen, and hydrogen-oxygen rocket propellant. The rims of these craters receive near-continuous sunlight, providing reliable solar energy. There is a finite amount of optimal terrain. Once it is occupied, it is occupied—there is no equivalent elsewhere on the Moon.

The nation that establishes infrastructure at these locations first will control the capacity for sustained human presence on the Moon. This is not merely a matter of prestige; it is a matter of power. Lunar-derived propellant could reduce the cost of deep-space missions by orders of magnitude, because launching mass from the Moon's shallow gravity well (1.62 m/s²) requires a fraction of the energy needed to escape Earth's gravity. Whoever controls the fuel depot controls the routes of expansion into the solar system.

The physics of orbital mechanics further favor the defender over the attacker in space. A nation with established infrastructure on the lunar surface or in cislunar orbit occupies the ultimate high ground. Objects launched from the Moon or from Lagrange points carry enormous kinetic energy relative to objects launched from Earth's surface, and the energy economics strongly favor the established position. To dislodge a power from a fortified lunar position would require an expenditure of resources orders of magnitude greater than what was needed to establish that position. This means that the window of opportunity for the United States to secure key locations is narrow and closing. Once China or another rival establishes a foothold, removing it becomes prohibitively expensive.

The United States Space Force, established in 2019, represents the institutional foundation for this mission, but it must be given a mandate that extends beyond satellite protection and missile warning. It must be developed into a force capable of projecting power throughout cislunar space—capable of defending American installations, deterring adversary aggression, and, if necessary, denying rival powers access to locations of critical strategic importance.

This is not warmongering. Deterrence is the surest guarantor of peace. The entire Cold War was dominated by the logic of deterrence: the certainty that aggression against American interests would be met with overwhelming force prevented the Soviet Union from translating its massive conventional military advantage in Europe into territorial conquest. The same logic applies in space. A credible American capacity to defend its territorial claims militarily is the single most effective means of ensuring that those claims are never tested.

V. The Economic Argument: Space Resources and National Prosperity

The economic potential of space resources is almost incomprehensibly vast. A single metallic asteroid of modest size—perhaps a kilometer in diameter—may contain more platinum-group metals than have ever been mined in human history. The Moon's reserves of helium-3, deposited over billions of years by the solar wind, could theoretically fuel fusion power plants producing clean energy for thousands of years. Water ice at the Lunar South Pole will become the most valuable commodity in the cislunar economy the moment permanent human habitation becomes a reality.

In a framework of exclusive territorial claims, the United States can grant mining rights, establish property protections, and create the legal certainty that is the precondition of private investment. The 2015 Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act already recognized the right of American citizens to own resources extracted from celestial bodies, but this right is meaningless without the sovereign power to enforce it against foreign competitors.

Consider the analogy of the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) framework established by the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. By granting coastal nations sovereign rights over resources within 200 nautical miles of their shorelines, the EEZ framework transformed chaotic, conflict-prone fisheries and seabed mining into manageable domains of national jurisdiction. It worked precisely because it acknowledged sovereign interests rather than pretending they didn't exist. An analogous framework in space—in which the United States and its allies claim exclusive economic zones around the installations they establish—would bring order to what will otherwise be a lawless frontier.

The economic benefits to the American public would be substantial. Revenue from space resource extraction could fund public services, reduce the national debt, and create entirely new industries. The technological spillovers from a national program of this ambition—comparable to those of the Apollo program, which generated technologies in computing, materials science, and telecommunications that drove decades of economic growth—would benefit every sector of the economy.

VI. The Cooperative Framework: The Artemis Accords as a Foundation

It is important to note that American territorial dominance in space need not be unilateral or exclusionary toward allies. The Artemis Accords, signed by over 40 nations as of 2024, already establish a framework for cooperative space exploration under American leadership. These accords include provisions for "safety zones" around lunar operations—a concept that comes remarkably close to soft territorial claims without explicitly violating the OST.

The model to follow is NATO: an alliance system in which the United States provides the security guarantee that enables its partners to operate safely. Allied nations—Australia, Japan, the United Kingdom, Canada, the European Space Agency's member states, and others—could operate within American-secured zones under agreements that provide access in exchange for political and logistical support. This would create a multilateral coalition with American security at its core, similar to the alliance structures that have maintained global stability since 1945.

This coalition model isolates adversarial powers like China and Russia, who have chosen to pursue their own lunar program outside the Artemis framework. Rather than pretending that the Sino-Russian International Lunar Research Station (ILRS) program is a benign scientific endeavor, the United States should treat it as what it is: a strategic challenge to American preeminence—and should respond accordingly.

VII. Addressing the Counterarguments

"This will start a war in space." Quite the opposite. Ambiguity and power vacuums start wars. Clear, enforceable claims backed by credible military power prevent them. No nation has attacked a NATO member precisely because the consequences are known and unacceptable. The same deterrence logic would apply in space.

"Space should belong to all humanity." This is a noble sentiment and poor policy. "All of humanity" is not a political actor. It cannot build infrastructure, enforce contracts, or defend territory. In practice, "space belongs to all humanity" means "space belongs to whoever gets there first and is ruthless enough to hold it." An American claim, embedded within an alliance structure and governed by democratic institutions, is the closest achievable approximation to a space domain that actually serves human interests broadly.

"This violates international law." International law is not a suicide pact. It is a framework that serves human interests, and when it ceases to do so, it must be reformed. The OST served its purpose during the Cold War. It is no longer fit for purpose. The United States has the prerogative—and the responsibility—to lead the construction of a new legal order that reflects current realities.

"Militarizing space is inherently dangerous." Space is already militarized. Every major power relies on satellites for communications, navigation, intelligence, and missile warning. China and Russia have both tested anti-satellite weapons. The question is not whether space will be a domain of military competition but whether the United States will lead that competition or cede it to adversaries.

VIII. Conclusion: The Burden of Leadership

The United States did not seek the role of global hegemon, but having assumed it, it has a responsibility not to abdicate it at the moment of greatest consequence.
